example.caption: Example answer
example.question: Does a virtual assistant answering customers on our website have to say that it is an artificial intelligence?
example.answer: Yes. Article 50(1) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 requires whoever provides an AI system meant to interact with people to design it so that people know they are talking to an AI, unless that is obvious from the context <ref1>[1]</ref1>. The obligation applies from {date} <ref2>[2]</ref2>.

method.title: Why you can trust a citation.
method.lead: A language model on its own invents plausible references. NormaAI makes it work on the text of the law and show its work.

1.title: Retrieval from the official text
1.body: The question searches the indexed acts for the relevant passages, by meaning and by exact words, with the corpus date stated.

2.title: An answer anchored to the passages
2.body: The model answers only from the retrieved passages and cites by act and article; the cited text stays visible next to the answer.

3.title: Every citation checked
3.body: Every citation shows whether the passage was found in the official text. If it was not, it is marked as unverified, not hidden.

4.title: Abstention when needed
4.body: If the retrieved passages are not enough, NormaAI says it cannot answer and suggests where to look, instead of filling the gap with an invention.

text.header: NormaAI scope check, rules and dates verified on {date}
text.disclaimer: A first indicative filter, not legal advice.

csrd.nonEuMissing: Enter the net turnover generated in the Union to assess the CSRD as a third-country company.
csrd.nonEuOverHeadline: The reporting regime for third-country companies may apply.
csrd.nonEuOverReason1: Net turnover in the Union: {amount}, above the {threshold} threshold the Codex gives for non-EU companies.
csrd.nonEuOverReason2: The Codex (ch. 1.2) also ties the obligation to a subsidiary or branch in the Union above 200 million euro: the check needs the group’s consolidated accounts and the turnover per Member State (ch. 2.4, case 2).
csrd.nonEuUnderHeadline: Below the EU turnover threshold for third-country companies.
csrd.nonEuUnderReason1: Net turnover in the Union: {amount}, below the {threshold} threshold (Codex, ch. 2.1).
csrd.nonEuUnderReason2: An Italian company controlled by the group may still be in scope as an EU subsidiary: in that case assess the subsidiary with the EU thresholds.
csrd.missing: Enter the average number of employees and the annual net turnover to assess the CSRD.
csrd.axisTurnover: Net turnover: {amount} ({over, select, yes {above} other {not above}} {threshold}).
csrd.inHeadline: The company is almost certainly within the scope of CSRD reporting.
csrd.inReason: You exceed both cumulative post-Omnibus thresholds: more than 1,000 employees and over 450 million euro of net turnover. Unless a specific exemption applies, you fall under the obligation to report on sustainability according to the ESRS.
csrd.inNote1: Check the exemptions: Wave 1 reporters (transitional exemption FY2025-2026) and group perimeters with holdings can change the picture.
csrd.inNote2: Double materiality and ESRS Set 1 (cut by about 61% of the datapoints) remain the core of the work: the reduction does not make the assessment simpler.
csrd.borderHeadline: Outside the CSRD obligation today, but on the edge of the threshold.
csrd.borderEmployees: You exceed the employee threshold but not the turnover one: since the rule is cumulative, you are outside the obligation today, but a rise in turnover or a change of perimeter is enough to bring you in.
csrd.borderTurnover: You exceed the turnover threshold but not the employee one: since the rule is cumulative, you are outside the obligation today, but net hiring or a consolidation can bring you in.
csrd.borderListed: As a listed company below the new size thresholds you are in principle excluded, but the position of a listed company has to be confirmed case by case (regulated-market obligations, group perimeter).
csrd.borderMargin: You are outside the obligation today, but close to a threshold: small changes in headcount, turnover or consolidation perimeter make you swing in and out from one financial year to the next.
csrd.borderCheck: This is the case where a precise check (and a choice between obligation, voluntary adoption and VSME) is worth the most.
csrd.borderNote1: Moving perimeter: scope is measured at year end, but ESG data must be collected over the whole year. With M&A or restructuring under way the analysis becomes multi-scenario.
csrd.borderNote2: Supply-chain pressure: even outside the obligation, customers in CSRD or CSDDD scope will ask you for disclosure (VSME) as a supplier.
csrd.outHeadline: Probably outside the scope of mandatory CSRD reporting.
csrd.outReason: You do not exceed the cumulative post-Omnibus thresholds (1,000 employees and 450 million euro of net turnover). The direct obligation is not triggered, but outside the CSRD does not mean outside everything.
csrd.outNote1: Supply-chain pressure (VSME): if you supply a group in scope, you will receive sustainability disclosure requests along the chain.
csrd.outNote2: Indirect Taxonomy: if you have bank financing, the bank (for its own GAR) may ask you for Taxonomy-eligibility data.
csrd.outNote3: Supply-chain CSDDD: the large groups bound to due diligence pass requirements on to their suppliers, well below their own direct thresholds.
csrd.noteWave1: You indicated reporting already under way (Wave 1, FY2024): Omnibus I provides a transitional exemption for the 2025 and 2026 financial years, after which the new thresholds apply again to the relevant year.
csrd.noteParent: Parent company: the figures are read on the consolidated accounts; for groups the basis is Art. 29a of Directive 2013/34/EU.
csrd.noteSubsidiary: Subsidiary: scope may depend on the consolidation perimeter and on the parent company’s reporting. A precise check at group level is needed.

csddd.nonEu: For third-country companies the available sources do not state the CSDDD thresholds: not assessed.
csddd.missing: Enter employees and net turnover to assess the CSDDD.
csddd.calendar: Transposition in the Member States by {transposition}, first application from {firstCompliance} (Directive (EU) 2026/470).
csddd.inHeadline: You also exceed the direct thresholds of the due diligence duty (CSDDD).
csddd.inReason: You exceed both cumulative post-Omnibus thresholds: more than 5,000 employees and over 1.5 billion euro of net turnover.
csddd.inNote1: Omnibus I removed the climate transition plan obligation and the harmonised civil liability regime, and replaced the full value-chain mapping with a general scoping exercise (Codex, ch. 1.4).
csddd.inNote2: Penalties: capped at 3% of worldwide net turnover (Codex, ch. 1.4).
csddd.outHeadline: Outside the direct thresholds of the due diligence duty (CSDDD).
csddd.outReasonOne: You exceed only one of the two cumulative thresholds: the direct obligation is not triggered today.
csddd.outReasonNone: You do not exceed the cumulative post-Omnibus thresholds (5,000 employees and 1.5 billion euro): the direct obligation is not triggered.
csddd.outNote: Supply-chain CSDDD: the large groups that are bound pass requirements on to their suppliers, well below their own direct thresholds. Disclosure requests along the chain arrive before the legal deadline.

aiAct.notAnswered: Answer the four AI questions to assess the transparency obligations of Art. 50.
aiAct.noneHeadline: From your answers, the transparency obligations of Art. 50 do not concern you directly.
aiAct.noneReason: None of the four situations of Art. 50 applies. Outside Art. 50 does not mean outside the AI Act.
aiAct.noneNote1: AI literacy (Art. 4): applicable from {date} to anyone who provides or uses AI systems: staff using AI must have an adequate level of competence.
aiAct.noneNote2: Prohibited practices (Art. 5): in force from {date} (for example harmful manipulation, social scoring, emotion recognition at work).
aiAct.noneNote3: General-purpose AI models: if you provide GPAI models, the Chapter V obligations apply from {date}, with enforcement powers from 2026.
aiAct.noneNote4: High risk: postponed, not cancelled. The rules apply from {annexIII} for stand-alone systems (Annex III) and from {annexI} for AI built into regulated products (Annex I); preparation takes months.
aiAct.inHeadline: From {date} Art. 50 covers the situations you indicated.
aiAct.inReason1: Mind who the addressee is: some obligations fall on whoever provides the system, others on whoever uses it. If your role is only that of deployer, the provider obligations fall on your provider, and vice versa.
aiAct.inReason2: The information must be given clearly and recognisably, at the latest at the first interaction or exposure (Art. 50(5)).
aiAct.inNote1: Penalties: up to 15 million euro or 3% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher; for SMEs and start-ups the lower of the two (Art. 99(4) and 99(6)).
aiAct.inNote2: In Italy, Law 132/2025 designates ACN (supervision and penalties) and AgID as national authorities for the AI Act.
aiAct.inNote3: What does not start on 2 August 2026: the rules on high-risk systems (Annex III), postponed to {date} by the digital Omnibus package.

chat.title: Chatbots and assistants: the person must know they are talking to an AI
chat.requirement: AI systems meant to interact directly with people must be designed and developed so that the person is informed they are interacting with an AI, unless this is obvious to a reasonably informed and attentive person.
chat.exception: Exception: systems authorised by law for law enforcement purposes, under certain conditions. If you buy the chatbot from a third party, the design obligation is the provider’s, but checking that it complies is in your interest.

gen.title: Generated content: machine-readable marking
gen.requirement: Providers of systems that generate synthetic content (audio, images, video or text) must ensure the outputs are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated; the technical solutions must be effective, interoperable, robust and reliable as far as technically feasible.
gen.exception: Exceptions: standard editing assistance functions or functions that do not substantially alter the input data, and uses authorised by law. Transitional: for generative systems already on the market before 2 August 2026 the marking applies from 2 December 2026; for new systems, 2 August 2026 applies. An EU Code of Practice on the transparency of AI content (10 June 2026, voluntary) supports implementation.

emo.title: Emotion recognition and biometric categorisation: inform the people exposed
emo.requirement: Whoever uses an emotion recognition or biometric categorisation system must inform the natural persons exposed to it about how the system operates, and process personal data in line with the GDPR.
emo.exception: Mind the prohibitions already in force (Art. 5, from 2 February 2025): for example emotion recognition in the workplace and in education institutions is prohibited, except for medical or safety reasons.

deep.title: Deepfakes and published AI texts: disclose their origin
deep.requirement: Whoever uses a system that generates or manipulates image, audio or video content constituting a deepfake must disclose that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated. The same applies to AI-generated texts published to inform the public on matters of public interest.
deep.exception: Exceptions: for evidently artistic, creative or satirical works the disclosure is given in an appropriate way that does not hamper the work; for texts, the obligation does not apply where there is human review or editorial control and a natural or legal person holds editorial responsibility.

privacy.title: Privacy Policy
privacy.intro: How NormaAI handles the personal data of the people who use the application, visit the site or write to us, under Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (GDPR).

p.1: NormaAI is a project by Daniel Culotta, a natural person, Inverigo (CO), Italy, not yet incorporated as a company. For any request about personal data write to <mail>info@normaai.org</mail>.
p.2: For the data an organisation enters in the application (users, companies analysed, documents, conversations) the organisation is the controller and Daniel Culotta is the processor under Art. 28 GDPR. A template data processing agreement is published in the code repository (folder docs/legal/) and can be requested at the same address.
p.3: For the data of those who visit the site, request the Codex or write by email, the controller is Daniel Culotta.

data.title: 2. Data processed
data.intro1: In the application, for registered users:

app.1: Account: email, name, password (stored only as a bcrypt hash), role, organisation, active status, creation date.
app.3: Clients, that is the companies analysed: name, sector, number of employees, turnover, jurisdictions, applicable regulations.
app.4: Conversations: questions and answers with their metadata (for example the sources cited), linked to the user and, where indicated, to the client.
app.5: Uploaded documents: the file is processed and deleted; what remains is the extracted text, in chunks indexed with the organisation identifier.
app.6: Assessments (gap analyses) and alerts generated for each client.
app.7: Event log: action, outcome, user, organisation, IP address, date and time.
app.8: The company profile filled in the forms is kept in the browser (sessionStorage) and sent to the API together with the question.

site.1: Codex or demo request: email, organisation name, role and originating form. When the request goes through the API, the IP address, user agent and referring page are also stored (to limit spam), together with the date and the number of downloads. When it goes through the serverless function on Vercel, the data is written to the function logs and emailed to info@normaai.org.
site.2: Email: the data contained in the messages sent to info@normaai.org.
site.3: Visit statistics: Vercel Web Analytics, without cookies and without identifying the visitor.

basis.title: 3. Legal basis and purposes

items.1: Providing the service and managing the account: performance of a contract (Art. 6(1)(b) GDPR).
items.2: Security of the service (event log, blocking of repeated sign-in attempts, rate limits, spam control): legitimate interest (Art. 6(1)(f) GDPR).
items.3: Sending the Codex and following up on the same subject with whoever requested it: legitimate interest (Art. 6(1)(f) GDPR). You can object at any time by replying to the email received or by writing to info@normaai.org.
items.4: Replying to those who write to us: legitimate interest or pre-contractual measures.

basis.p: The data is neither sold nor used for advertising profiling. It is shared only with the providers listed in section 4, to deliver the service.

processors.title: 4. Sub-processors and providers

items.1: Hetzner Online GmbH (Germany): the server running the API and the databases. The application data stays in the European Union.
items.2: Vercel Inc. (USA): hosting of the site and the interface, in the Frankfurt region, and the serverless function that receives Codex requests. Visit statistics without cookies.
items.3: Google LLC (Gemini API, USA): the language model that generates the answers. It receives the question, the company profile if entered and the retrieved passages of law. It is the default provider; the code allows Anthropic or OpenRouter to be configured instead.
items.4: Resend, Inc. (USA): sending of transactional emails (Codex delivery, notification of new requests).
items.5: Cloudflare, Inc.: DNS management of the normaai.org domain only, without proxying the traffic. It handles DNS queries, not content.

processors.p: For providers based in the United States, transfers rely on the standard contractual clauses included in their data processing agreements.

items.1: Application data: for the whole duration of the relationship. There is no automatic deletion on expiry. The organisation’s administrator can export the data and delete clients, conversations, assessments, alerts and indexed chunks from the application at any time; every user can delete their own conversations. To close the accounts and the organisation write to info@normaai.org.
items.2: Backups: the database is copied every night and the copies are kept for 30 days on the server. Deleted data may remain in a backup for up to 30 days.
items.3: Codex requests: kept in the database until deletion is requested. The download link expires after 30 days.
items.4: Event log: in the server logs, with their rotation.
items.5: Data in the browser: see the <cookie>cookie policy</cookie>.

p.1: You can request access, rectification, erasure, restriction, portability and object to processing by writing to <mail>info@normaai.org</mail>. You can also lodge a complaint with the Italian data protection authority (Garante per la protezione dei dati personali).
p.2: In the application, without writing to us: the administrator can export all the organisation’s data in JSON and erase its contents; every user can delete their own conversations.
p.3: If your data was entered by an organisation that uses NormaAI (for example as an analysed client company), the request goes to that organisation, which is the controller; if it reaches us, we forward it.

p.1: NormaAI uses a generative language model (Google Gemini by default) to write the answers from the passages of law retrieved from the corpus, built from EUR-Lex and Normattiva (CSRD, CSDDD, AI Act, DORA, NIS2, EU Taxonomy, GDPR, CRA). All outputs are generated by an artificial intelligence system, may contain errors and need to be checked by a professional. The notice appears in the application, on the Ask page and in the reports.
p.2: NormaAI makes no automated decisions with legal effects on people: it produces analyses that a professional evaluates.

scope.title: 1. What this page covers
scope.p: Cookies are small text files that sites save on the device. This page also covers the browser’s similar technologies, localStorage and sessionStorage, which NormaAI uses for the same technical purposes.

cookies.title: 2. Cookies
cookies.p1: NormaAI sets a single technical, first-party cookie, which remembers the interface language. No third-party, profiling or marketing cookies. Authentication and the other preferences use the browser’s local storage described below.

storage.title: 3. Local storage in the browser
storage.p1: All keys are first-party, written and read only by normaai.org, and serve the operation of the site and the application. None is used to track or profile.
storage.p2: Keys in localStorage (they stay until you delete them; the first three are deleted by sign-out):
storage.p3: Keys in sessionStorage (deleted by the browser when the tab is closed):

thirdParty.title: 4. Third-party tools
thirdParty.p1: The site loads Vercel Web Analytics, which uses neither cookies nor local storage and collects aggregate visit statistics without identifying the visitor. There are no other third-party scripts: no Google Analytics, Tag Manager, advertising pixels or social plugins. The fonts are served from our own domain.
thirdParty.p2: If tools using cookies or identifiers were introduced in the future, this page would be updated and consent would be asked before activation.

basis.title: 5. Legal basis and consent
basis.p: Strictly technical storage, such as the language cookie, is exempt from prior consent under Art. 122 of the Italian Privacy Code (Legislative Decree 196/2003) and the guidelines of the Italian data protection authority (Decision No 231/2021). That is why NormaAI shows no accept-or-reject banner: it shows a notice with a link to this page and the "Got it" button.

manage.title: 6. How to manage the storage
manage.p: You can delete the data from the browser settings (site data). Signing out deletes the tokens and the demo flag. If you block local storage, access to the reserved area does not work, because the session tokens are kept there; without the language cookie the site goes back to Italian.

contacts.title: 7. Contact
contacts.p: For any request about data processing write to <mail>info@normaai.org</mail>. See also the <privacy>Privacy Policy</privacy>.

security.title: Security
security.intro: The security measures present in the NormaAI code and those still missing. The code is public: every section names the files it is taken from, so whoever has to assess us can check instead of trust.

hosting.title: 1. Where the site, the API and the data run
hosting.p1: The public site and the application interface are hosted on Vercel, in the fra1 region (Frankfurt). The API and the databases (PostgreSQL for the data, Qdrant for search, Redis for cache and sessions) run on a Hetzner server in Germany.
hosting.p2: In production the only service exposed to the internet is Caddy, which terminates TLS with Let’s Encrypt certificates (ports 80 and 443) and forwards requests to the application on an internal network. The application has no public ports, runs in a container without root privileges, with a read-only filesystem and no additional Linux capabilities.

model.title: 2. The language model
model.p1: The answers are written by a third-party language model. By default it is Google Gemini (setting llm_provider equal to gemini, a model of the Gemini 2.5 Flash family). To generate an answer, the question, the company profile if entered and the passages of law retrieved from the corpus are sent to the model provider, which processes them on its own systems.
model.p2: The provider can be changed in the configuration: the code also supports Anthropic and OpenRouter. Today there is no mode in which the answers are generated entirely on our servers.

access.title: 3. Access and sessions

items.1: You sign in with email and password. Passwords are stored only as bcrypt hashes with an individual salt.
items.2: The password check takes the same time even when the email does not exist, so neither response times nor error codes reveal which accounts exist.
items.3: After 5 failed attempts, access for that email is blocked for 5 minutes.
items.4: Sessions use JWT tokens signed with RS256: a private key signs, a public key verifies. In production the application refuses to start without RSA keys. The access token lasts 60 minutes, the refresh token 7 days.
items.5: Every renewal invalidates the previous token. If a token already used is presented again, the whole token family is revoked and the user has to sign in again. Signing out revokes the tokens in use.
items.6: The list of revoked tokens is in Redis. In production, if Redis does not respond, tokens are rejected rather than accepted.
items.7: Three roles: admin, member, viewer. API calls are rate-limited per user or, if anonymous, per IP address.
items.8: In the browser the tokens are kept in localStorage and deleted at sign-out (see the <cookie>cookie policy</cookie>).

access.p: There is no two-factor authentication and no SSO: see section 11.

isolation.title: 4. Separation between organisations
isolation.p: Each organisation sees only its own data, and the separation is enforced by the database, not only by the application.

items.1: PostgreSQL has Row Level Security policies on users, clients, conversations, assessments and alerts: every row is visible only in the session of the organisation it belongs to.
items.2: The application connects with a dedicated non-superuser role (normaai_app), because PostgreSQL ignores the policies for superusers and table owners. In production, if the connected role is a superuser, the application refuses to start.
items.3: The organisation context is set on every transaction and cleared when the connection goes back to the pool: it cannot leak from one request to the next.
items.4: The answer cache uses keys that include the organisation: an answer computed for one client is never served to another.
items.5: In the search engine every chunk of an uploaded document carries the organisation identifier. A search returns the organisation’s chunks plus the shared regulatory corpus; a search without an organisation returns only the shared corpus, never other people’s documents.
items.6: A test with two organisations runs in CI on PostgreSQL with a non-superuser role and fails the build if one organisation sees the other’s data.

documents.title: 5. Uploaded documents
documents.p1: An uploaded document (PDF, HTML or image, up to 50 MB) is written to a temporary file, processed and deleted at the end of processing, even if it fails. What remains is the extracted text, split into chunks and indexed in the search engine with the organisation identifier.
documents.p2: The organisation’s administrator can export all the organisation’s data in JSON and delete clients, conversations, assessments, alerts and indexed chunks in bulk. Deletion requires explicit confirmation and is recorded in the event log.

headers.title: 6. HTTP headers, CORS and IP addresses

items.1: The site sends Content-Security-Policy, X-Content-Type-Options, X-Frame-Options (DENY), Referrer-Policy, Permissions-Policy and Strict-Transport-Security. The API sends the same headers (HSTS in production) and does not expose the server name.
items.2: CORS accepts only the origins listed in the configuration. In production a wildcard origin prevents start-up.
items.3: The client IP address, used for rate limits and for the event log, is read from the position added by our proxy and not from the first value of X-Forwarded-For, which anyone can forge.

links.title: 7. Signed download links
links.p: Whoever requests the Codex receives a link signed with HMAC-SHA256 and valid for 30 days. The signature is verified with a constant-time comparison; an expired or altered link is rejected. The public form is rate-limited per IP address.

audit.title: 8. Event log
audit.p1: Successful and failed sign-ins, sign-outs, token renewals and reuses, creation and deletion of clients and conversations, questions, document uploads, exports and erasures are recorded as structured events with user, organisation, IP address, date and time and outcome.
audit.p2: Today these events end up in the application logs on the server. There is no separate long-term archive yet and no export ready for auditors: retention is that of the server logs.

backup.title: 9. Backups
backup.p1: A script started by cron every night at 02:00 runs pg_dump of the PostgreSQL database in compressed format, checks that the archive is readable with pg_restore --list and keeps the copies for 30 days in the backups/ folder of the same server.
backup.p2: The script neither encrypts the file nor copies it to another system: the weekly copy to external storage is a documented manual procedure, not an automatic one. Qdrant and Redis are not backed up: the index is rebuilt with a new indexing, the cache is ephemeral by design. The restore procedure is documented in the repository.

items.1: The code is public on <github>GitHub</github> under the MIT licence.
items.2: On every push and pull request the CI runs ruff (lint and format), mypy (blocking on the authentication, database and audit modules), the backend tests on real PostgreSQL, Qdrant and Redis, type-check, tests and build of the frontend, the Docker image build with a Trivy scan, Gitleaks on the whole git history, Bandit and the generation of a CycloneDX SBOM.
items.3: CodeQL analyses Python and JavaScript/TypeScript with the security-extended queries on every push to the main branch and every week.
items.4: On every release the image is blocked if Trivy finds critical or high vulnerabilities, and the SBOM is attached to the release. Dependabot proposes dependency updates.
items.5: .env files and .pem keys are excluded from the repository; the CI fails if it finds API keys or private keys in tracked files.

items.1: No SSO (SAML or OpenID Connect) and no two-factor authentication: you sign in with email and password only.
items.2: No SOC 2 or ISO 27001 certification and no formal third-party penetration test. The automatic scans in CI do not replace it.
items.3: No encryption at rest managed by the application: data protection on disk is that of the server.
items.4: No long-term archive of the event log and no automatic backup copy outside the server.
items.5: The prompt injection filter records the attempts but does not block the input. The real defence is structural: the user’s text never enters the system prompt and the citations are checked against the retrieved passages.

report.title: 12. Reporting a vulnerability
report.p1: Write to info@normaai.org with the subject [SECURITY] NormaAI, explaining how to reproduce the problem and its impact. Do not open a public issue on GitHub.

items.3: Fix or mitigation of critical and high reports within 30 days.
items.4: No monetary reward; credit in the release notes, if welcome.

report.p2: Only the main branch and the latest published release receive security fixes.
report.p3: For security questionnaires or for the template data processing agreement (Art. 28 GDPR, in the docs/legal/ folder of the repository) write to the same address.

metodo.metaDescription: How a NormaAI answer is made: EUR-Lex and Normattiva corpus with a stated date, hybrid retrieval, source-grounding checks, abstention when the text is not enough. Every claim points to the public code file that implements it.
metodo.title: How an answer is made, and when it does not come.
metodo.intro: We publish the method and the code. This page describes the pipeline as it is today, without counters and without promises: every section points to the files of the public repository that implement it, so you can verify instead of believe.

corpus.title: The corpus: official texts, with a date
corpus.p1: There are two sources: EUR-Lex, queried through the SPARQL endpoint of the Publications Office of the European Union, and the Normattiva Open Data for the Italian transposition. The texts are split by article and indexed; every chunk keeps the act (CELEX or URN), the article, the section title and the date.
corpus.p2: The acts in the acquisition list:

1.name: CSRD
1.acts: Dir. (EU) 2022/2464, ESRS (Delegated Reg. (EU) 2023/2772), the stop-the-clock directive (Dir. (EU) 2025/794) and Omnibus I (Dir. (EU) 2026/470)

8.name: CRA
8.acts: Reg. (EU) 2024/2847 and Implementing Reg. (EU) 2025/2392, the latest addition to the list

corpus.p3: The corpus does not update by itself. The periodic acquisition cycle exists in the code but is off by default: the corpus is re-indexed through explicit operations, and the reference date (corpus_as_of) is set at deploy time, returned in the metadata of every API answer and printed in the footer of the reports. Texts superseded by later acts are excluded from the search by default.

pipeline.title: The pipeline, step by step
pipeline.lead: Every question goes through these steps in order. The numbers quoted are the thresholds set in the code, not measured results.

1.title: Hybrid retrieval
1.body: The question is searched in two ways at once: by meaning, with dense vectors of the multilingual model paraphrase-multilingual-mpnet-base-v2 (768 dimensions, chosen because the corpus mixes the English of EUR-Lex and the Italian of Normattiva), and by exact terms, with BM25-style sparse vectors that capture "Article 29" or a CELEX number. The two rankings are merged with Reciprocal Rank Fusion, with no weights to tune. Filters exclude superseded texts and limit the search to the shared corpus plus the organisation’s documents.

2.title: Drafting from the retrieved text
2.body: The model receives the question, the company profile if entered and the retrieved passages, with the instruction to cite act and article and not to invent acts or articles that do not exist. The user’s text never enters the system prompt. The default model is Google Gemini, configurable.

3.title: Several samples, one decision
3.body: To calibrate confidence, the system generates several independent answers (3 by default) and groups them by behaviour. The result is a computed confidence score, not one self-declared by the model: above 0.85 the answer passes; below 0.50, or if not even two samples agree, the system abstains and says so, asking for an expert review. If the best retrieved evidence is weak (dense similarity below 0.25), the answer is flagged for review anyway and confidence is capped.

4.title: Source-grounding check
4.body: Every citation in the answer is compared with the retrieved passages: the regulation, the CELEX numbers in the text, the article number and the quoted sentence must exist in the evidence. An unsupported citation does not block the answer, but marks it as "expert review needed" and lowers the confidence. The check runs on the draft and again on the answer actually served.

5.title: Chain-of-Verification, on request
5.body: A five-stage verification exists (claim extraction, verification questions, revision, validation of CELEX and URN references against EUR-Lex and Normattiva), but it is off by default and is enabled per request, only for answers with confidence below 0.85. It is not applied to every answer.

6.title: In progress: deterministic verification
6.body: We are introducing a deterministic citation check, that is an exact comparison of the quoted passage with the indexed official text, which does not depend on a model. Until it is in production, it stays on this page as work in progress, not as a fact.

items.1: The act and the article cited, the passage quoted and the link to the official text.
items.2: A reliability level expressed in words, not a percentage.
items.3: The "expert review needed" flag when the system abstains, finds weak evidence or an unsupported citation.
items.4: The notice that the answers are generated by an artificial intelligence system (Reg. (EU) 2024/1689, Art. 50): in the application footer, on the Ask page and in the reports.

data.title: Data and separation between organisations
data.p1: The site is on Vercel (Frankfurt region); the API and the databases on a Hetzner server in Germany. Each organisation sees only its own data: Row Level Security in PostgreSQL with a non-superuser role, per-organisation cache keys, per-organisation filter in the search engine. The administrator can export and erase the organisation’s data from the application.
data.p2: The details, and what is still missing (SSO, certifications, penetration test), are on the <securityPage>Security</securityPage> page.

ci.title: How we check the code
ci.p1: On every push: lint and format (ruff), type-check (mypy, blocking on the security modules), backend tests on real PostgreSQL, Qdrant and Redis, including a test with two organisations that fails the build if one sees the other’s data; type-check, tests and build of the frontend; CodeQL, Gitleaks, Bandit, Trivy and an SBOM.
ci.p2: Test counts change with every commit: that is why we do not print them here. They can be read in the latest CI run on the repository.

choices.title: Choices you can read in the code
choices.lead: The decisions that matter are annotated next to the code that implements them, even when they correct a mistake of ours.

1.title: Multilingual embedding model
1.body: The English-only embedding model degraded search over Italian legal text. Switching to the multilingual model required re-indexing the whole corpus, because the vectors live in a space specific to the model.

2.title: Stated corpus date
2.body: The corpus is frozen between one re-indexing and the next, and the "superseded" status of an act is set only at that stage. Until repeal detection is automatic, the honest mitigation is to state the corpus date in every answer and in every report.

3.title: Periodic update switched off
3.body: A periodic acquisition cycle existed on paper but did not really run. It is now explicitly off by default, until a dedicated process manages it: better an explicit, dated re-indexing than an untrue "updated every night".

4.title: Optional Chain-of-Verification
4.body: The five-stage verification adds further model calls for every answer. It is available on request, not promised on everything: the always-on checks are multiple sampling and source grounding.

5.title: Cyber Resilience Act on the list
5.body: The CRA was added to the acquisition list together with the implementing regulation on product categories, noting the application dates next to the CELEX numbers (reporting obligations from 11 September 2026, full application from 11 December 2027).

cta.title: Judge the method on a real question.
cta.lead: Bring a real case from your work. If the answer, citations in hand, is no better than your current research, it ends there.
